title: Sentence completion – Fair trade and working conditions

instruction.text: You are listening to a speech given at an international conference on social justice. The speaker is pointing out the importance of fair trade and working conditions. Listen to the audio file below and fill in the blanks.
instruction.sound: You are listening to a speech given at an international conference on social justice. The speaker is pointing out the importance of fair trade and working conditions. Listen to the audio file below and fill in the blanks.

hint.text: Tippe auf die Lücken, um zwischen den Lücken zu springen und die möglichen Antworten anzuzeigen.

atoms.a: <voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>Good afternoon everyone! Thank you for giving me the opportunity to speak today. My name is Maya Torres, and I have spent the past ten years working with organizations that fight for fair working conditions around the world. When we talk about globalization, we often celebrate it as a driver of economic growth and innovation. But behind many of the products we use every day — from our morning coffee to the clothes we wear — lies a story of injustice that too often goes untold.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>Let’s start with a simple fact: around 138 million children are still engaged in child labour worldwide, according to the International Labour Organization. Many of them work in supply chains that serve Western markets. A T-shirt that costs five euros might seem like a great bargain, but its low price often hides exploitation — workers in textile factories in Bangladesh or Ethiopia sometimes earn less than two dollars a day. They work 10 to 14 hours, often without proper safety equipment or healthcare. These conditions are not exceptions. They are part of a global economic system that rewards the lowest production cost rather than human dignity.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>Fair Trade offers a concrete alternative. It is not charity — it’s about justice. Fair Trade standards ensure that workers receive fair wages, have safe working conditions, and are allowed to form unions. Farmers and producers are paid a minimum price that covers the cost of sustainable production, plus a Fair Trade premium that communities can invest in schools, healthcare, or clean water. In the cocoa industry, for instance, certified producers can earn up to 20–30% more than those selling through conventional markets. That difference is life-changing — not only for the workers but for entire communities.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>But here’s the truth: change doesn’t just depend on companies or governments. It depends on us — the consumers. Every time we buy a product, we make a choice about the kind of world we want to support. Surveys show that 72% of European consumers say they care about ethical production, yet only a fraction consistently buy Fair Trade goods. If more people turned those values into action, companies would have a powerful incentive to change their supply chains.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>At the same time, consumer choices alone are not enough. We also need stronger laws to hold corporations accountable. Initiatives like the EU’s proposed Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive aim to require companies to identify and address human rights violations in their supply chains. This is a crucial step, but it faces strong opposition from industry groups. We must push our governments to put people before profit and enforce standards that protect workers globally.</voice><voice voiceLang='en' voice='f6Us_chirp'>To conclude, globalization doesn’t have to mean exploitation. It can mean shared prosperity — if we make it so. But this requires all of us: governments that legislate responsibly, companies that value people over profit, and consumers who demand fairness with their wallets. Every small decision — from the chocolate we buy to the clothes we wear — is a vote for the kind of world we want to live in. Let’s make sure that world is just, humane, and sustainable.</voice>
atoms.b:
Maya Torres is an activist that advocates for ((++human_rights climate_justice)) and fair ((++working_conditions industrial_standards)).
According to the ILO, around ((++138_million 183_million)) children are still involved in child labour worldwide. Maya Torres points out that labor is performed under ((++high_risk good_conditions)) for workers.
Fair Trade standards guarantee not only fair wages but also ((++safe_working_conditions assured_holidays)) and the right to ((++form_unions wear_safety_gear)).
Although about ((++72% 17%)) of European consumers say they care about ethical production, only a small percentage consistently act accordingly.
The proposed EU Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive would require companies to ((++identify_and_address completely_avoid)) human rights violations in their supply chains.
The speaker argues that each small consumer decision, such as ((++buying_chocolate_or_clothes investing_in_fair_trade_startups)), is a vote for a fairer world.
